- multiple light-emitting devices, each equipped with a position sensor that identifies the device’s position with respect to at least one reference point established independently of the lighting scene;
- at least one of the light-emitting devices additionally equipped with an orientation sensor for sensing its orientation, a luminaire-classification sensor for identifying its type, or both; and
- a controller configured to transmit control instructions to the light-emitting devices so that they collectively produce the lighting scene.

The lighting system comprises multiple illumination sources configured to create a coordinated lighting scene within a user-occupied environment. Each illumination source includes a location sensor that detects the source’s position relative to at least one reference point established independently of the lighting scene.

At least one illumination source further includes an orientation sensor, a luminaire-type sensor, or both. The orientation sensor determines the direction in which the source is aimed, while the luminaire-type sensor identifies relevant characteristics of the source, such as its optical configuration or light-distribution pattern.

A controller uses the detected location of each illumination source, together with its orientation and/or luminaire type, to determine the location at which the source’s illumination effect will appear. Based on the relative positions of the illumination sources, their projected effects, and the independently defined reference point, the controller adapts the commands sent to the sources. In this way, the lighting scene is rendered consistently relative to the reference point, even if individual illumination sources are moved, reoriented, or replaced.
outputs.L4:
A lighting system includes one or more illumination sources configured to generate respective illumination effects within an environment. Each illumination source is associated with one or more sensors capable of determining the source’s location, orientation, luminaire type, or other operating characteristics. The sensors may be incorporated into the illumination source, mounted on or near the source, or otherwise associated with it. Sensor data is communicated to a controller, which may be located locally within a luminaire, distributed among multiple luminaires, or implemented as a central lighting controller.

The controller uses the sensor data to determine the position and direction of each illumination effect relative to a reference point or coordinate system defined independently of the physical placement of the illumination sources. The reference point may correspond, for example, to a stage, room, display, object, user-selected origin, or virtual coordinate system. Based on the measured location and orientation of a source, as well as information identifying its luminaire type and optical characteristics, the controller can determine how a command will affect the position, shape, color, intensity, and direction of the resulting illumination effect.

Lighting-scene commands may therefore be expressed with respect to the independent reference point rather than in terms of fixed control values for particular luminaires. Before transmitting or executing those commands, the controller adapts them for the current configuration of each illumination source. Such adaptation may include transforming coordinates, adjusting pan and tilt values, selecting or modifying beam parameters, compensating for differences in optical output, or assigning an intended effect to a suitable luminaire. The controller may repeat this process when a source is moved, rotated, replaced, or reconfigured.

As a result, a desired lighting scene can be rendered accurately without requiring each illumination source to occupy a predetermined position, have a predetermined orientation, or be of a particular luminaire type. The same scene definition may be reused across different installations and may remain valid after changes to the lighting arrangement. This reduces manual programming and calibration while allowing illumination effects to maintain their intended spatial relationship to the independently defined reference point.
outputs.L5:
## A Lighting System

A lighting system is an essential part of any home, office, or public space. It provides visibility, improves safety, and creates a comfortable atmosphere. A well-designed lighting system usually combines different types of light, including general lighting for overall brightness, task lighting for specific activities, and accent lighting to highlight architectural features or decorative objects.

Modern lighting systems often use energy-efficient LED technology. LED lights consume less electricity, last longer, and require less maintenance than traditional bulbs. Smart controls, motion sensors, timers, and dimmers can further reduce energy use while allowing users to adjust brightness and color according to their needs.

When designing a lighting system, it is important to consider the purpose of the space, the availability of natural light, and the comfort of its users. Effective lighting should minimize glare and shadows while providing adequate illumination. By combining functionality, efficiency, and thoughtful design, a lighting system can make a space safer, more attractive, and more enjoyable.

a plurality of luminaires, each luminaire configured to emit light in response to a respective control signal;

a localization subsystem configured to determine, for each luminaire, a location of the luminaire relative to a fixed reference point and, for at least one of the luminaires, at least one of an orientation or a luminaire type; and

control the plurality of luminaires using the respective control signals to render the lighting scene relative to the fixed reference point.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide patent-style wording for a lighting arrangement in which luminaires include position sensors, at least one luminaire also senses orientation or type, and a central controller uses those measurements to calculate effect locations and adapt scene-control commands.
counterfactuals.output:
### Exemplary Independent Apparatus Claim

1. **A lighting arrangement comprising:**

a plurality of luminaires, each luminaire comprising at least one light source, a position sensor configured to provide position information representative of a position of the respective luminaire, and a communication interface;

at least one of the plurality of luminaires further comprising a characteristic sensor configured to provide characteristic information representative of at least one of an orientation of the respective luminaire and a type of the respective luminaire; and

a central controller communicatively coupled to the plurality of luminaires, the central controller being configured to:

receive the position information from the plurality of luminaires and the characteristic information from the at least one luminaire;

determine, based at least on the received position information and characteristic information, respective effect locations at which light effects produced by the plurality of luminaires are expected to occur within an illuminated environment;

receive or generate a scene-control command specifying at least one desired lighting effect at a target location; and

adapt the scene-control command, based on the determined effect locations, to generate respective luminaire-control commands for causing one or more of the plurality of luminaires to produce the desired lighting effect at or in relation to the target location.

### Exemplary Dependent Claims

2. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the characteristic information comprises an orientation expressed as at least one of a tilt angle, a pan angle, a roll angle, or a three-dimensional orientation vector.

3. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the type information identifies at least one of an optical distribution, a beam angle, a light-output characteristic, a luminaire model, a mounting configuration, or an available lighting-effect function.

4. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein each effect location comprises a point, an area, a volume, a beam axis, or a projected beam footprint.

5. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the central controller determines an effect location by applying an optical model associated with a luminaire type to a measured position and a measured or inferred orientation of the respective luminaire.

6. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein adapting the scene-control command comprises selecting one or more luminaires according to a spatial relationship between their respective effect locations and the target location.

7. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein adapting the scene-control command further comprises modifying at least one of intensity, color, color temperature, beam width, beam direction, timing, transition rate, or activation state.

8. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the central controller recalculates at least one effect location in response to detecting a change in the position, orientation, or type of a luminaire.

9. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the position sensor comprises or cooperates with at least one of a satellite-positioning receiver, an indoor-positioning receiver, a radio-frequency ranging device, an optical positioning device, an ultrasonic positioning device, an inertial sensor, or a localization beacon.

10. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the central controller stores a spatial representation of the illuminated environment and associates each luminaire with its determined effect location in the spatial representation.

11. The lighting arrangement of claim 1, wherein the central controller is configured to compensate automatically for relocation, replacement, or reorientation of at least one luminaire without requiring modification of the scene-control command.

### Exemplary Method Claim

12. **A computer-implemented method of controlling a lighting arrangement comprising a plurality of luminaires, the method comprising:**

receiving, from position sensors associated with respective luminaires, position measurements indicative of positions of the luminaires;

receiving, from at least one of the luminaires, a measurement or identifier indicative of an orientation or a type of the at least one luminaire;

calculating, using the position measurements and the measurement or identifier, effect locations associated with light effects producible by the luminaires;

obtaining a scene-control command defining a desired lighting effect with reference to a target location;

adapting the scene-control command according to the calculated effect locations; and

transmitting luminaire-control commands resulting from the adaptation to selected ones of the luminaires.

### Exemplary Specification Wording

The disclosed arrangement enables scene-control information to be expressed independently of the physical placement or configuration of individual luminaires. Position information supplied by the luminaires, together with orientation and/or type information supplied by at least one luminaire, is used by a central controller to determine where the optical effect of each luminaire will occur. The controller may thereby translate a location-based scene description into device-specific control instructions. If a luminaire is moved, rotated, replaced, or reconfigured, the controller may update the corresponding effect location and adapt subsequent scene-control commands so that the intended spatial lighting effect is maintained.

### Exemplary Abstract

A lighting arrangement includes a plurality of luminaires having respective position sensors and communication interfaces. At least one luminaire further provides information indicative of its orientation and/or luminaire type. A central controller receives the position and orientation or type information and calculates locations at which lighting effects produced by the luminaires are expected to occur. The controller adapts scene-control commands based on the calculated effect locations and generates luminaire-specific commands for producing a desired lighting effect at a target location. The arrangement may automatically compensate for relocation, reorientation, or replacement of a luminaire.
